newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Data and position squaring.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Data and position squaring.

text.p: U.S. credit markets will have some fresh data to chew on Thursday while players put final touches on their trading strategies ahead of the key employment report on Friday, analysts said.
"It's not going to be a day for bravery coming in the doorstep of the employment report," said Dana Johnson, managing director of fixed-income research at First National Bank of Chicago.
Prices are seen mostly rangebound as participants square portfolios and play defense ahead of the key figure.

"Usually in the runup to the employment report we have position-squaring, which I think, in this case, would argue for a little bit of defensiveness," Johnson said. "The market has lately been trading long."
Analysts said the yield of the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond is expected to trade in a fairly large range between 6.35 and 6.45 percent on Friday.

Treasuries fell Wednesday after a lack of a coupon pass by the Federal Reserve combined with a weaker dollar against the yen and a falling stock market cast a shadow on the bulls. The bond fell 14/32 at 101-11 in late trade to yield 6.40 percent.
"I think we'll continue to trade in ranges tomorrow (on Thursday)," said Kevin Flanagan, economist and first vice-president at Dean Witter Reynolds.

On the economic indicator front, the market will take in initial jobless claims for the week ended November 30. In a Reuters poll, economists see claims sliding, on average, to 337,000 against 342,000 in the previous period.

The government will then release its revised figures for third quarter productivity at 1000 EST/1500 GMT. The number is expected to be revised down to a negative 0.1 percent against a preliminar 0.2 percent rise.
The revised numbers for unit labor costs in the third quarter are expected to be released on Thrusday at 1000 EST/1500 GMT as well.

Analysts said Treasuries will also take its cues from other financial markets, such as stocks and foreign exchange. A close eye is to be kept in the performance of the dollar against the Japanese yen.

"We'll continue to watch the dollar ... It's interesting to know that over the last couple of days you've seen three major financial markets move lower in tandem," Flanagan said, referring to Treasuries, stocks and the dollar versus the yen.
The market will also take in some fresh supply on Thursday, when the Treasury will offer some $19.25 billion of 52-week bills.
The bidding deadline is set for 1300 EST/1800 GMT.
"I think the supply will end up being absorbed by the market. But that is not to say it can't put some downward pressure on prices," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.

The Federal Reserve injected temporary reserves into the banking system on Wednesday through overnight system repurchase agreements when the federal funds were traded at 5-5/16 percent, above the central bank's 5-1/4 percent target.
The Fed refrained once again from injecting permanent reserves to the system through an expected coupon pass operation. Analysts said, however, they still believe the move may take place on Thursday.
Fed funds are seen opening at 5.30 percent on Thursday.
